--- PAGE 1 ---
AI Act Compliance  Assistant  
Objective  
Build a multi -agent application that analyzes one AI use case at a time  using uploaded use -case 
documents and a built -in EU AI Act reference corpus . 
The system should produce a grounded first -pass assessment with citations, identify missing 
information and uncertainties, and support follow -up questions through chat.  
Challenge Overview  
Users should be able to create an analysis session for one AI use case and upload multiple 
supporting documents describing it, such as case studies, vendor white papers, technical 
overviews, product descriptions, policy documents, or internal process notes . The system should 
synthesize these inputs into a single case understanding.  
System should : 
• summarize the use case  
• extract relevant facts  
• retrieve relevant EU AI Act material  
• generate an initial assessment  
• show citations and supporting evidence  
Users should not need to upload the EU AI Act or related guidance themselves. These should 
already be available in the application as a built -in reference corpus.  
Scope  
The core analysis should cover:  
• whether the described technology appears to qualify as an AI system  
• possible EU AI Act risk classification , including sector - or product -specific AI Act 
considerations where relevant  
• prohibited -practice, transparency, labelling, and GPAI obligations, where relevant  
• possible roles, such as provider or deployer  
• missing information and uncertainties  
• practical compliance -related requirements and governance measures under the EU AI Act  
In this challenge, “governance” means different structures, tools, and processes used to manage 
AI’s effects and mitigate risks through the lens of what is required by the EU AI Act. These may 
include, for example, documentation, monitoring mechanisms, ris k management processes, and 

--- PAGE 2 ---
human oversight mechanisms.  
 
EU data legislation, national implementation, and other adjacent legal frameworks may be 
included as bonus capabilities, but they should be clearly separated from the core AI Act 
analysis. Sector - or product -specific considerations may be included where th ey are relevant 
within the scope of the AI Act.  
Suggested Reference Corpus  
Required  
• EU AI Act – official Regulation text  
http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj  
Recommended  
• Commission guidelines on prohibited AI practices  
https://digital -strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission -publishes -guidelines -
prohibited -artificial -intelligence -ai-practices -defined -ai-act 
• Commission guidelines on AI system definition  
https://digital -strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission -publishes -guidelines -ai-
system -definition -facilitate -first-ai-acts-rules -application  
• Commission Code of Practice on Marking and Labelling of AI -generated Content  
https://digital -strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission -publishes -second -draft -code -
practice -marking -and-labelling -ai-generated -content  
• Implementation documents list  
https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/implementation -documents/  
Optional  
• General -Purpose AI Code of Practice  
https://digital -strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/contents -code -gpai 
• EU AI Act Explorer  
https://artificialintelligenceact.eu  
• Finnish implementation context  
Traficom: https://traficom.fi/fi/tekoalyn -saantely/tietoa -eun-tekoalyasetuksesta  
TEM: https://tem.fi/tekoalyasetus  
Valtioneuvosto: https://valtioneuvosto.fi/hanke?tunnus=TEM044:00/2024  
Teams may use other reliable sources, but should clearly label the source type, such as 
legislation, official guidance, national implementation material, commentary, or uploaded use -
case material.  
Core Requirements  

--- PAGE 3 ---
The system should:  
• support one AI use case per session  
• allow multiple uploaded documents per use case  
• use a built -in EU AI Act -focused corpus  
• generate an initial analysis without requiring the user to write their own prompt or query  
• cite uploaded and reference sources  
• support follow -up chat in the same session  
• separate facts, references, assumptions, uncertainties, and system -generated interpretation  
• avoid presenting outputs as final legal advice  
Expected Output  
The analysis should include:  
1. Use-case summary  
A concise summary based on the uploaded documents.  
2. Extracted facts  
Key facts such as purpose, users, affected persons, sector, input data, outputs, automation 
level, human oversight, deployment context, use of AI -generated content, use of GPAI, 
and possible impact on people.  
3. Preliminary EU AI Act assessment  
A reasoned first -pass assessment with relevant citations, including whether the system 
appears to meet the AI Act definition of an AI system, possible risk classification, 
transparency or labelling obligations, GPAI obligations, and uncertainties.  
4. Governance observations  
Practical notes on , for example,  documentation, risk management, transparency, human 
oversight, monitoring, logging, accountability, and role clarity.  
5. Missing information and follow -up questions  
Gaps that prevent a confident assessment and questions an expert might ask next.  
6. Citations and evidence separation  
A clear distinction between uploaded -document facts, regulatory references, optional 
sources, assumptions, and system reasoning.  
Multi -Agent Requirement  
Participants should implement a multi -agent workflow where agents have distinct 
responsibilities, exchange intermediate outputs, and show some degree of autonomous behavior.  
The system should not simply be a fixed linear prompt chain. Agents should be able to make 
context -dependent decisions, such as:  
• deciding which uploaded -document facts are relevant for AI Act analysis  
• choosing which reference materials to retrieve  
• identifying when more evidence is needed  

--- PAGE 4 ---
• flagging contradictions, missing information, or weak evidence  
• deciding when to ask follow -up questions  
• triggering a critique or review step when the assessment is uncertain  
• revising the analysis based on new information from the user  
Teams may design their own architecture, but should explain what each agent does, what 
decisions it can make autonomously, how agents communicate, and how the system avoids 
unsupported or overconfident conclusions.  
Bonus Capabilities  
Teams can receive bonus points for useful additions beyond the core requirements, such as:  
• detecting when EU data legislation, national implementation rules, or other adjacent legal 
frameworks may also be relevant  
• retrieving newer AI Act implementation updates  
• adding Finnish implementation context  
• providing a dedicated analysis path for GPAI definitions and obligations  
• asking targeted follow -up questions and updating the assessment  
• showing confidence or uncertainty levels  
• creating role -based outputs  
• generating a checklist of next steps and documentation needs  
• exporting the analysis as a report  
• adding a critique or red -team agent  
• flagging source quality and type  
• comparing several use cases at portfolio level  
Evaluation  
Solutions will be evaluated on:  
• Content quality : correct use -case understanding and identification of relevant AI Act 
concepts   
• Regulatory grounding : use of relevant EU AI Act sources, accurate mapping between 
source material and the assessment, and useful citations  
• Multi -agent design : meaningful agent roles, autonomous behavior, intermediate outputs, 
and justified workflow  
• User experience : usability, clarity, and useful follow -up chat  
• Technical implementation : document handling, retrieval quality, and session context  
• Transparency of output : clear distinction between facts, assumptions, system reasoning, 
uncertainties, and limitations  
• Innovation : creative and practical approaches to the core workflow, user experience, 
agent design, evidence handling, or bonus capabilities  
Note to Participants  

--- PAGE 5 ---
The EU AI Act is new, and its practical interpretation is still developing. There is currently no 
court -case precedent directly interpreting it.  
Your system should be transparent about evidence, uncertainty, assumptions, and reasoning. The 
goal is to build a decision -support tool for structured review, not a final compliance authority .

assessment.summary: The AI Act Compliance Assistant is a proposed multi-agent system designed to evaluate individual AI use cases against the EU AI Act framework. By ingesting user-provided documentation, the system generates a structured compliance analysis, identifies regulatory obligations, and highlights gaps or uncertainties, while avoiding the provision of final legal advice.

extracted_facts.purpose: To provide a grounded, first-pass compliance assessment of AI use cases against the EU AI Act.
extracted_facts.users: Compliance officers, AI developers, or legal professionals assessing AI systems.
extracted_facts.sector: Cross-sector (all sectors subject to the EU AI Act).
extracted_facts.input_data: User-uploaded documentation including case studies, white papers, technical overviews, product descriptions, policies, and internal process notes.
extracted_facts.outputs: Structured analysis report including use-case summary, extracted facts, EU AI Act risk classification, governance observations, and follow-up questions.
extracted_facts.automation_level: Multi-agent autonomous workflow with human-in-the-loop chat interactions.
extracted_facts.human_oversight: The system acts as a decision-support tool; final interpretation and compliance decisions rest with the human user.
extracted_facts.use_of_generative_ai: Yes. The system is described as a multi-agent application that generates textual analysis and assessment reports.
extracted_facts.use_of_gpai: No. The system is designed to assess GPAI obligations, but it is not inherently a GPAI model itself.
extracted_facts.impact_on_people: The system provides decision support for compliance; its output impacts the governance and legal alignment of AI systems, indirectly affecting those subject to those AI systems.

is_ai_system.reasoning: The system acts as a multi-agent autonomous workflow utilizing generative AI to infer from user-provided documentation. It generates complex analytical content and recommendations based on input, satisfying the Article 3(1) criteria of machine-based operation, autonomy in processing, and generation of content that influences the user's compliance environment.
citations: Article 3(1) - Definition of an AI System

risk_classification.reasoning: The system does not fall under prohibited practices (Article 5) nor does it qualify as High-Risk under Annex III (it does not perform recruitment, credit scoring, education, or law enforcement functions). It serves as a general-purpose, non-critical decision-support tool. It is not a GPAI model itself, as it is a specific tool built to *assess* such models, not a foundation model trained at scale for general utility.

role_assessment.reasoning: The entity developing this system for use by compliance officers and legal professionals is placing an AI-enabled software tool on the market. Under Article 3, the entity developing the software is the Provider, regardless of the fact that it leverages third-party models.

legal_obligations.scope: Disclosure to users that they are interacting with an AI system and that the content is AI-generated.
legal_obligations.relevance: The system uses generative AI to produce reports; users must be informed of the AI-generated nature of the analysis.
citations: Article 50 - Transparency obligations for certain AI systems

governance_observations.risk_management: Implement basic quality assurance processes to verify the accuracy of the generated compliance reports, given the high legal stakes of the outputs.
governance_observations.data_governance: Ensure that sensitive user-uploaded documentation is not used to retrain the underlying models, preventing potential data leakage or loss of privilege/confidentiality.
governance_observations.documentation: Maintain clear 'Instructions for Use' stating that the system is a decision-support tool, not a substitute for legal advice.
governance_observations.human_oversight: Mandatory 'human-in-the-loop' requirement; the system output must be explicitly validated by a qualified legal professional before any compliance filing is made.
governance_observations.logging_and_monitoring: Maintain logs of generated outputs for internal auditing and quality improvement, even if not strictly required under high-risk Article 12.

adjacent_frameworks.gdpr_overlap: If the system processes personal data contained in the user-uploaded documentation, Article 35 (DPIA) may be required depending on the volume and sensitivity of the data handled.
adjacent_frameworks.finnish_context: The Finnish Data Protection Ombudsman monitors AI systems for GDPR compliance, particularly in relation to automated processing of personal information.
adjacent_frameworks.european_context: Compliance must align with the EU AI Office guidance on transparency and any specific sectoral guidelines from national authorities such as the CNIL or AEPD if the system processes personal data of citizens within those jurisdictions.

citations.title: Article 3(1) - Definition of an AI System
citations.relevance_summary: Establishes the criteria for machine-based autonomy and inference used to qualify the system.

citations.title: Article 50 - Transparency obligations
citations.relevance_summary: Mandates disclosure of AI-generated content for systems interacting with natural persons.

assessment.critic_summary: The assessment relies on a potentially flawed assumption that the tool is 'Minimal Risk' without fully evaluating the implications of it acting as an 'AI system' that influences high-risk decisions. By positioning itself as a tool for compliance professionals, the system could inadvertently facilitate the certification of high-risk AI models; if the tool's output is flawed, it could lead to systematic compliance failures. The analysis lacks a robust investigation into whether the 'multi-agent' nature triggers additional obligations under GPAI or if the system could be misconstrued by users as a replacement for expert legal counsel, thereby creating liability.

ai_system_definition.justification: The definition is robust; it clearly qualifies as an AI system under the Article 3(1) criteria of inference and automated processing.

risk_classification.justification: The 'Minimal Risk' label is highly speculative. It fails to consider the potential for the system to be categorized as a 'safety component' if it is used to validate high-risk AI systems or if its guidance directly leads to a breach of the EU AI Act.

roles_and_obligations.justification: The provider role is correctly identified, but the analysis ignores potential 'deployer' risks if the company uses its own tool to self-assess its other AI products.

flagged_assumptions.assumption: The system remains 'Minimal Risk' regardless of the criticality of the AI systems it is assessing.
flagged_assumptions.risk: If the tool provides a 'green light' for an Annex III system, the tool itself could be viewed as part of the conformity assessment process, potentially elevating its own risk profile.

flagged_assumptions.assumption: Users will consistently treat this as a decision-support tool and not a definitive legal authority.
flagged_assumptions.risk: Over-reliance (automation bias) is a well-documented risk. If users treat outputs as fact, the liability for erroneous compliance advice remains legally complex.

information_gaps.impact: Without knowing if user documentation is processed on-premise, in a private cloud, or via public LLM APIs, it is impossible to confirm GDPR/AI Act data privacy compliance.
If the system learns from user-provided compliance assessments, it may be creating a risk of data poisoning or propagating incorrect legal interpretations across the user base.

expert_followup_questions: How does the system ensure that the 'multi-agent' architecture maintains source traceability back to the EU AI Act text for every claim made?
Does the system implement a 'manual override' for the classification engine, and is that override auditable?

If the system processes confidential internal company data (e.g., source code or trade secrets) as part of the 'documentation,' what cryptographic or technical measures prevent these from being ingested into the base model's long-term memory?
Does the system provide a disclaimer that meets the specific formatting requirements for Article 50 (Transparency) in a way that cannot be ignored by the user?

source_quality_audit.notes: Primary legal source; the analysis uses the correct OJ reference.
Relevant for local context, but the assessment lacks evidence that these guidelines are directly applicable to an AI compliance tool.
This is a critical blindspot; the auditor assumes a low-risk classification without performing a sub-clause check for Annex III systems.

uncertainties: Specific deployment environment (e.g., cloud vs. on-premises).
Technical architecture and specific LLMs used to drive the multi-agent system.
Targeted audience profile beyond general compliance users.
Handling of sensitive or confidential user-uploaded data.

chat_history.content:
### Initial Assessment Compiled!
Our multi-agent system has completed the compliance audit for your use case.

**Summary of findings:**
- **AI System Qualification:** True
- **Assessed Risk Level:** Minimal Risk
- **Compliance Role:** Provider

Please review the tabs in the main workspace for a full breakdown. I am ready to answer any questions, retrieve specific texts, or update this analysis if you have new details!
WHAT ARE THE RISKS WITH THIS USE CASE

As a decision-support tool, the primary risks associated with this use case center on **automation bias** and **legal liability**. Because this system provides guidance on regulatory compliance, there is a risk that users might over-rely on its outputs without verifying them against the actual text of the EU AI Act. If the system misinterprets an obligation or incorrectly categorizes a high-risk system as 'minimal risk,' it could lead the user to unintentionally bypass mandatory conformity assessments, exposing them to significant enforcement actions or legal liabilities.

Furthermore, there are inherent **data security risks** regarding the documentation you upload. Since the system ingests potentially sensitive internal files, policies, or proprietary process notes, there is a risk of data leakage or privacy violations if these inputs are stored insecurely or used to train external models. Mismanagement of this data could lead to breaches of GDPR or the loss of trade secrets, which are not currently covered under the AI Act but are critical for your organizational security.

Finally, the 'multi-agent' nature of the system introduces **traceability risks**. If the AI fails to cite its internal reasoning or misrepresents the legal basis for a conclusion, you lack the 'human-in-the-loop' visibility required to challenge or correct its output. We recommend implementing rigorous audit logging and maintaining a strict 'human-validation-required' policy for all generated compliance reports to mitigate these concerns.
